```{r}
#| label: cov-values
#| include: false
# Numbers quoted in the prose, read from the output files.
read_out <- function(...) {
  utils::read.csv(
    here::here("..", "output", ...),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
    fileEncoding = "UTF-8"
  )
}
f1 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1)
f2 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)
f3 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3)
big <- function(x) format(round(x), big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE)
span <- function(x, f = f2) {
  if (length(unique(f(x))) == 1L) f(x[[1L]]) else paste(f(min(x)), "to", f(max(x)))
}
and_list <- function(x) {
  if (length(x) < 2L) return(paste(x))
  paste(paste(x[-length(x)], collapse = ", "), "and", x[[length(x)]])
}
hours <- function(t) sub("h$", " h", t)
pct <- function(x) paste0(round(100 * x), "%")
rule_label <- c(
  "shrinkage, per type" = "per-type shrinkage",
  "shrinkage, common" = "common shrinkage",
  "two-parameter, per type" = "the per-type two-parameter arm",
  "two-parameter, common" = "the common two-parameter arm",
  "factor, per type" = "per-type factor analysis",
  "factor, shared loadings" = "shared loadings"
)

# Panels and units (output/grn/plugin/)
gene_sets <- read_out("grn", "plugin", "gene_sets.csv")
panel_n <- function(gs) {
  table(factor(gene_sets$time_point[gene_sets$gene_set == gs], c("48h", "72h", "96h")))
}
n_welch <- panel_n("welch")
n_r2_01 <- panel_n("r2_01")
n_r2_05 <- panel_n("r2_05")
pairs_m <- n_welch * (n_welch - 1) / 2 / 1e6
units_w <- read_out("grn", "plugin", "plugin_summary.csv")
units_w <- unique(units_w[units_w$gene_set == "welch", c("time_point", "cell_type", "cells")])
cells_time <- tapply(units_w$cells, units_w$time_point, sum)
rank_w_96 <- cells_time[["96h"]] - sum(units_w$time_point == "96h")
unit_name <- function(time, type) paste0(tolower(type), " (", hours(time), ")")
unit_the <- function(time, type) paste0("the ", hours(time), " ", tolower(type))

# Tuning values chosen on held-out cells, Welch panel
cv_date <- format(
  file.mtime(here::here("..", "output", "grn", "cv", "cv_selected_tuning.csv")),
  "%d %B %Y, %H:%M"
)
sel_w <- read_out("grn", "cv", "cv_selected_tuning.csv")
sel_w <- merge(
  sel_w[sel_w$gene_set == "welch", ], units_w,
  by.x = c("time", "cell_type"), by.y = c("time_point", "cell_type")
)
rule_of <- function(r) sel_w[sel_w$rule == r, , drop = FALSE]
shr_w <- rule_of("shrinkage, per type")
is_epi48 <- shr_w$time == "48h" & shr_w$cell_type == "Epiblast"
epi48 <- shr_w$tuning[is_epi48]
shr_rest <- shr_w[!is_epi48, ]
lam_big <- shr_rest$tuning[shr_rest$cells >= 1000]
lam_small <- shr_rest$tuning[shr_rest$cells < 1000]
common_w <- unique(rule_of("shrinkage, common")[c("time", "tuning")])
common_w <- common_w[order(common_w$time), ]
one_se_diag <- rule_of("shrinkage, per type, 1se")
one_se_diag <- one_se_diag[one_se_diag$tuning >= 1, ]
tp_type <- rule_of("two-parameter, per type")
tp_all <- rbind(tp_type, unique(rule_of("two-parameter, common")))
fa_w <- rule_of("factor, per type")
fa_top <- fa_w[fa_w$tuning == max(fa_w$tuning), ]
fa_small <- fa_w[fa_w$cells < 1000, ]
shared_w <- unique(rule_of("factor, shared loadings")[c("time", "tuning")])
shared_w <- shared_w[order(shared_w$time), ]

# Nested comparison, Welch panel
nested_w <- read_out("grn", "cv", "nested_cv_summary.csv")
nested_w <- merge(
  nested_w[nested_w$gene_set == "welch" & nested_w$rule != "diagonal", ], units_w,
  by.x = c("time", "cell_type"), by.y = c("time_point", "cell_type")
)
n_positive <- sum(nested_w$mean_gain_over_diagonal > 0)
n_two_se <- sum(nested_w$mean_gain_over_diagonal > 2 * nested_w$se_gain)
weak <- nested_w[nested_w$mean_gain_over_diagonal <= 2 * nested_w$se_gain, ]
weak_txt <- and_list(paste0(
  rule_label[weak$rule], " for ", unit_the(weak$time, weak$cell_type),
  " (", round(weak$mean_gain_over_diagonal), ", se ", round(weak$se_gain), ")"
))
best_w <- do.call(rbind, lapply(
  split(nested_w, paste(nested_w$time, nested_w$cell_type)),
  function(d) d[which.max(d$mean_gain_over_diagonal), ]
))
best_w <- best_w[order(-best_w$cells), ]
borrow <- best_w$rule %in% c(
  "factor, shared loadings", "two-parameter, per type", "two-parameter, common"
)
by_fold <- read_out("grn", "cv", "nested_cv_by_fold.csv")
by_fold <- by_fold[
  by_fold$gene_set == "welch" &
    by_fold$rule %in% c("shrinkage, common", "two-parameter, common"),
]
n_common_choices <- nrow(unique(by_fold[c("time", "rule", "outer_fold")]))
diag_folds <- unique(by_fold[by_fold$tuning >= 1, c("time", "rule", "outer_fold")])
best_txt <- function(d) {
  and_list(paste0(
    unit_name(d$time, d$cell_type), ", ", rule_label[d$rule],
    " (", round(d$mean_gain_over_diagonal), ")"
  ))
}

# Search comparison (archived stage; output/grn/cv/search_comparison.csv)
search <- read_out("grn", "cv", "search_comparison.csv")
s_of <- function(a, s, d = search) d[d$arm == a & d$strategy == s, , drop = FALSE]
s_med <- function(a, s, k, d = search) stats::median(s_of(a, s, d)[[k]])
grid_d <- s_of("shrinkage", "grid, one factorisation per value")
grid_worst <- grid_d[which.max(grid_d$score_loss), ]
opt_d <- s_of("shrinkage", "optimiser on the path")
search_w <- search[search$gene_set == "welch", ]
scores <- read_out("grn", "cv", "cv_tuning_scores.csv")
n_levels <- length(unique(scores$tuning[scores$arm == "shrinkage"]))

# Information criteria, Welch panel
ic <- read_out("grn", "cv", "information_criteria.csv")
ic <- ic[ic$gene_set == "welch", ]
ic_best <- function(d) {
  data.frame(
    time = d$time[[1L]], cell_type = d$cell_type[[1L]],
    aic = d$rank[which.min(d$aic)], bic = d$rank[which.min(d$bic)],
    top = max(d$rank)
  )
}
ic_fa <- ic[ic$arm == "factor", ]
ic_type <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(ic_fa, paste(ic_fa$time, ic_fa$cell_type)), ic_best))
ic_sh <- ic[ic$arm != "factor", ]
ic_shared <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(ic_sh, ic_sh$time), ic_best))
bic_high <- ic_type[ic_type$bic > 8, ]

# Deconvolution at the chosen levels (output/deconvolution/lambda_selection.csv)
lsel <- read_out("deconvolution", "lambda_selection.csv")
lsel <- lsel[lsel$arm == "standard" & lsel$gene_set == "welch" & lsel$time == "96h", ]
rmse_id <- function(id) lsel$rmse[lsel$id == id][1L]
bulk_pick <- lsel[lsel$family == "shrinkage" & lsel$selected_profile, ][1L, ]

# Choices made once per time, three panels
sel_all <- read_out("grn", "cv", "cv_selected_tuning.csv")
shared_all <- unique(sel_all[sel_all$rule == "factor, shared loadings", c("gene_set", "time", "tuning")])
common_all <- unique(sel_all[sel_all$rule == "shrinkage, common", c("gene_set", "time", "tuning")])
shared_top <- max(scores$tuning[scores$arm == "factor_shared"])
bulk_lam <- read_out("deconvolution", "lambda_selection.csv")
bulk_lam <- bulk_lam[bulk_lam$arm == "standard" & bulk_lam$family == "shrinkage" &
  bulk_lam$selected_profile %in% TRUE, c("gene_set", "time", "tuning")]
bulk_wr <- bulk_lam$tuning[bulk_lam$gene_set %in% c("welch", "r2_01")]
bulk_05 <- bulk_lam[bulk_lam$gene_set == "r2_05", ]
bulk_05 <- bulk_05[order(bulk_05$time), ]

# Second-pass results (output/deconvolution/second_pass/)
sp <- read_out("deconvolution", "second_pass", "benchmark_metrics.csv")
denoised_96 <- mean(sp$rmse[
  sp$method == "DeCovarT denoised (bio only) | lbfgsb | b_g none | welch" & sp$time == "96h"
])
first_pass <- read_out("deconvolution", "second_pass", "plugin_summary_first_pass.csv")
first_pass <- first_pass[first_pass$gene_set == "welch", ]
```

## Scope and status {#sec-cov-scope}

[Numbers to rerun: they were computed on the panel of the earlier tier (i), which dropped the 2,178 mostly fractional genes and used the 5 % presence gate. Tier (i) now keeps every gene and applies the gate of @eq-fs-presence (@sec-fs-qc-applied).]{.highlight}

This chapter estimates, for each scored cell type $j$ at each
bulk-matched time, the mean $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}$ and
the within-type covariance $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j}$ of the
gene panel of tier (ii) (@sec-fs-consistency), and exports them on the
linear scale of DeCovarT's convolution,

$$
\bigl\{
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j},\,
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j},\,
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Omega}}_{j}=\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j}^{-1}
\bigr\}_{j=1}^{J},
\qquad
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j}\succ 0 .
$$ {#eq-grn-export}

The target is the covariance that enters the likelihood, not a
mechanistic gene network; a dense estimate is therefore an acceptable
plug-in
([3.2, why a regularised covariance](https://bastienchassagnol.github.io/DeCovarT/articles/03-2-covariance-network-estimation.html#nte-cov-why)).

**What is run.** `scripts/03_05_stats_plugin_covariance.R` stores the
sample moments of every type; it regularises nothing. The deconvolution
builds each covariance from these moments with `build_sigma()`, for one
`r glossary("arm")` and one tuning value. Every arm keeps the sample
variances and regularises the correlation (@sec-cov-estimators). The
tuning values are chosen here, on held-out cells (@sec-cov-cv-run), or
by the bulk likelihood (@sec-deconv-selection), always by
`r glossary("grid search")`. The sparse-precision arms and the
denoised covariance are archived (@sec-cov-archived). The theory is in
[3.2, estimators](https://bastienchassagnol.github.io/DeCovarT/articles/03-2-covariance-network-estimation.html#tbl-cov-estimators).

| Step | Code | Output |
|---|---|---|
| Estimators, held-out scores, `build_sigma()` | `R/03_01_stats_covariance_estimation.R` | functions only |
| Sample moments per time × gene set | `scripts/03_05_stats_plugin_covariance.R` | `output/grn/plugin/`: `gene_sets.csv`, `plugin_summary.csv`, `moments_<time>_<gene_set>.rds` (not in Git) |
| Tuning on held-out cells, nested comparison, factor fits | `scripts/03_04_cv_covariance.R` | `output/grn/cv/`: five CSV tables (@sec-cov-cv-run), `factors_<time>_<gene_set>.rds` (not in Git) |
| Search comparison (archived stage) | `scripts/archives/search_comparison/` | `output/grn/cv/search_comparison.csv`, kept and read by @tbl-cov-search |

: Covariance-estimation code and outputs. {#tbl-cov-status}

### Inputs and scales {#sec-cov-inputs}

Every arm reads the raw UMI counts of the scored cells, element
`slots[[time]]` of `output/feature_selection/tier_01/scored_slots.rds`
(@sec-fs-qc-applied): `counts` (genes × cells), `cell_type`, `batch`
and `library_size`, the full RNA library of each cell. The counts are
restricted to the genes of
`output/feature_selection/tier_02/selected_<time>.csv`, the panel gated
by the permuted Welch $G$ at BH 0.05 (@sec-fs-consistency), the
`r glossary("Welch panel")`: `r big(n_welch[["48h"]])` genes
at 48 h, `r big(n_welch[["72h"]])` at 72 h and
`r big(n_welch[["96h"]])` at 96 h, with no cap.
`read_panel_slot()` does the subset and returns cells × genes. The
500-gene legacy export of @sec-fs-export is no longer read.

Three gene sets per time are listed in `output/grn/plugin/gene_sets.csv`:
`welch`, the whole gated panel; `r2_01`, its genes with a
`r glossary("deviance share")` $R^2_D\ge 1\%$
(`r and_list(big(n_r2_01))` genes at 48, 72 and 96 h); and `r2_05`,
those with $R^2_D\ge 5\%$ (`r and_list(big(n_r2_05))` genes). Results in
this chapter are on the Welch panel unless stated. For each time and gene set,
`sample_moments()` writes the mean of each type (`mu`), its unbiased
sample covariance, not regularised (`sigma_sample`), its number of
cells (`n_cells`), and the pooled within-type correlation of the time
(`r_pool`, @sec-cov-two-param). `plugin_summary.csv` lists, per unit,
the cells, the genes and the genes constant within the type; on the
Welch panel no gene is constant within a type.

**Normalisation.** The exported means and covariances are computed on
raw per-cell UMI counts, with no per-cell library division
(`normalise = "none"`). Dividing each cell by its total library removes
the type-level transcriptome size $S_j$: signatures become mRNA
fractions, and the proportions are estimated as
$q_j\propto p_jS_j$ instead of $p_j$
[@luTranscriptomeSizeMatters2025, p. 13]. It also removes the biological
`r glossary("cell size")` variation between cells of one type, which
the bulk accumulates. Without spike-ins the technical
`r glossary("size factor")` cannot be separated from
the biological one, so the size term of the covariance was bracketed by
the coefficient $\kappa$ of the denoised estimator, now archived
(@sec-cov-archived):
$\kappa=0$ treats all size variation as biological;
$\kappa=\hat\nu/(1+\hat\nu)$ treats it all as technical, which matches
library normalisation for the covariance. The argument is in
[3.2, raw or denoised](https://bastienchassagnol.github.io/DeCovarT/articles/03-2-covariance-network-estimation.html#sec-raw-vs-denoised).
The earlier per-cell division, `X <- y / (lib / ref_lib)` with
`ref_lib` the median library of the time point, was a sensitivity
variant (`normalise = "library"`) of the archived code. The archived
`PLNnetwork` arm kept its full-library offset $\log s_c$ in both cases.

**Size term removed alone.** `sample_moments(..., library_size = )`
gives the "all technical" end of the $\kappa$ bracket without the rest
of the denoised estimator. The mean is kept on raw counts; the
covariance is computed on the cells of type $j$ divided by their size
factor $L_c/\bar L_j$, with $L_c$ the full library of cell $c$ and
$\bar L_j$ its mean over the type. That removes the size term
$\nu\,\mu_g\mu_h$ and keeps the Poisson diagonal, which the archived
denoised covariance also removed. This is the size-normalised input of
the scale screen of chapter 4 (@sec-deconv-scale-screen).

Means and covariances are computed on the linear counts, never on
$\log(1+x)$: the convolution is linear only on an additive scale
([2.1, normalisation](https://bastienchassagnol.github.io/DeCovarT/articles/02-1-single-cell-generative-optimisation.html#sec-norm-linear)).
An earlier glasso script fitted and exported on $\log(1+x)$; that
choice was reverted before it was archived.

### Units and regimes {#sec-cov-units}

Each fit uses the cells of one type at one time, treated as
independent draws: eleven type × time units (@tbl-fs-cell-counts).
Cell line is not a covariate (@sec-geo-design). The panel has $G_t$
genes at time $t$, before genes constant within a type are removed.
@tbl-cov-units sets the $C_j$ cells of each unit against three
sample-size layers
([3.2, regimes](https://bastienchassagnol.github.io/DeCovarT/articles/03-2-covariance-network-estimation.html#sec-cov-regimes)):
existence of the maximum-likelihood estimate of
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}$, support recovery by the graphical lasso, and
support recovery by neighbourhood selection.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-cov-units
#| tbl-cap: "The eleven type × time units against the gated panel. $C_j$: scored cells of the unit (`cell_counts.csv`); $G_t$: panel genes at that time (rows of `selected_<time>.csv`). The two recovery columns are orders of magnitude without their constants, with natural logarithms and an assumed maximum node degree $d=10$ of the precision graph; they are not thresholds. Shaded rows ($C_j\\le G_t$) have a singular sample covariance and need a regularised estimate."
#| echo: false
fs_dir <- here::here("..", "output", "feature_selection")
units <- utils::read.csv(
  file.path(fs_dir, "tier_01", "cell_counts.csv"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  fileEncoding = "UTF-8"
)
units <- units[units$scored, , drop = FALSE]
units <- units[order(units$time_point, -units$cells), , drop = FALSE]
times <- unique(units$time_point)
panel_size <- vapply(
  times,
  function(tm) {
    nrow(utils::read.csv(
      file.path(fs_dir, "tier_02", paste0("selected_", tm, ".csv")),
      fileEncoding = "UTF-8"
    ))
  },
  integer(1)
)
d <- 10 # assumed maximum degree of the precision graph
g <- unname(panel_size[units$time_point])
glasso_order <- d^2 * log(g)
neighbour_order <- d * log(g)
fmt <- function(x) format(round(x), big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE)
yes_no <- function(x) ifelse(x, "yes", "no")
tab <- data.frame(
  sub("h$", " h", units$time_point),
  units$cell_type,
  fmt(units$cells),
  fmt(g),
  yes_no(units$cells >= g + 1),
  fmt(glasso_order),
  yes_no(units$cells > glasso_order),
  fmt(neighbour_order),
  yes_no(units$cells > neighbour_order)
)
colnames(tab) <- c(
  "Time",
  "Cell type",
  "$C_j$",
  "$G_t$",
  "MLE of $\\boldsymbol{\\Sigma}_j$ exists ($C_j\\ge G_t+1$)",
  "$d^{2}\\log G_t$",
  "$C_j>d^{2}\\log G_t$",
  "$d\\log G_t$",
  "$C_j>d\\log G_t$"
)
singular <- which(units$cells <= g)
tinytable::tt(tab) |>
  tinytable::group_tt(
    j = list(
      "Graphical-lasso support recovery" = 6:7,
      "Neighbourhood selection" = 8:9
    )
  ) |>
  tinytable::format_tt(quarto = TRUE) |>
  tinytable::style_tt(j = c(3, 4, 6, 8), align = "r") |>
  tinytable::style_tt(i = singular, background = "#fbe3d6")
```

```{r}
#| label: cov-units-values
#| include: false
mle <- units$cells >= g + 1
neither <- units$cells <= neighbour_order & units$cells <= glasso_order
units_txt <- function(i) {
  and_list(paste0(
    tolower(units$cell_type[i]), " at ", hours(units$time_point[i]),
    " (", big(units$cells[i]), " cells against ", big(g[i]), " genes)"
  ))
}
```

In `r sum(units$cells <= g)` of the `r nrow(units)` units
$C_j\le G_t$: the sample covariance is singular, and only a regularised
estimate exists. Only the `r units_txt(which(mle))` have a
maximum-likelihood estimate. The graphical-lasso order is exceeded by
`r sum(units$cells > glasso_order)` units and the
neighbourhood-selection order by `r sum(units$cells > neighbour_order)`;
`r and_list(unit_the(units$time_point[neither], units$cell_type[neither]))`
exceed neither. The cross-validated
score of @sec-cov-cv-run is defined in every regime because each arm
returns a positive definite matrix.

### Bulk depth per cell {#sec-cov-bulk-depth}

Which covariance enters the bulk law, raw or denoised, depends on the
bulk depth per cell relative to the reference
([3.2, raw or denoised](https://bastienchassagnol.github.io/DeCovarT/articles/03-2-covariance-network-estimation.html#sec-raw-vs-denoised)):
the raw covariance is exact only at $a_i=1$. For bulk sample $i$,

$$
a_i=\frac{y_{+i}/n_i}{\bar s_{\mathrm{ref}}},
$$ {#eq-cov-bulk-depth}

<!-- chk: V45 -->

with $y_{+i}$ the total counts of the bulk sample, $n_i$ the
`r glossary("cell count", "number of cells")` in it, and
$\bar s_{\mathrm{ref}}$ the median UMIs per reference cell at the
matched time; $a_i$ is the `r glossary("capture ratio")` of the
sample. $a_i<1$ is expected: the bulk library is
deeper in total than one droplet, but it spreads that depth over every
cell of the pooled sample. Bulk counts are reads, not UMIs, so their
sampling noise is overdispersed, with a dispersion $\omega_i\ge1$ that
lowers the effective depth to $a_i/\omega_i$. The raw plug-in, the
implemented default, assumes $a_i=1$. $n_i$ is
[TODO: cells per gastruloid × gastruloids per bulk sample, from the Suppinger et al. 2023 methods]{.highlight}
[@suppingerMultimodalCharacterizationMurine2023, STAR Methods, p. 25].
How a count $n_i$ would enter the scale models of the deconvolution is
in @sec-deconv-scale-models.

::: {.highlight}
**TODO: number of cells per bulk sample, $n_i$.**

What the paper gives (STAR Methods, p. 25): each bulk sample is one
batch of 96 gastruloids, each seeded from 300 mESCs (EmbryoMax
129/SvEv). RNA was extracted on RNeasy columns, and 1,000 ng
entered the Illumina stranded mRNA library. The 18 runs of
PRJNA954338 hold 19–32 million read pairs (2 × 74 bp). Neither the
number of cells per gastruloid at 48, 72 and 96 h nor the total RNA
yield per sample is reported.

Two definitions of $n_i$ must not be confused. The cells whose RNA
entered the library are $n_i=1{,}000\ \mathrm{ng}/m_{\mathrm{RNA}}$,
with $m_{\mathrm{RNA}}$ the total RNA per gastruloid cell. That is at
most $96\,N_t$, with $N_t$ the cells per gastruloid at time $t$, and
equals it only if the whole extract went into the library.

Candidate sources for $N_t$:

- Frenster et al. (2026), *Nat. Cell Biol.* 28:875–889,
  doi:10.1038/s41556-026-01923-x. They give absolute cell counts per
  gastruloid by flow cytometry, with growth curves (Fig. 2m–n, Extended
  Data Fig. 4e–f) for gastruloids seeded from 300 mESCs. The values
  appear only in the figures (or in the source data), which are still
  to be read.
- "A fluctuation test for gastruloid heterogeneity", *Cell* (2026),
  S0092-8674(26)01203-1. A search snippet attributes to it reference
  values of about 15,000–20,000 cells per gastruloid at 120 h and about
  30,000 at 144 h. Unverified: the page was not readable, and the
  primary source of those numbers is unknown.
- Fiuza et al., bioRxiv 10.1101/2024.12.12.628151 (seeding from 20 to
  600 cells). It gives no counts against time in the text read so far.

Neither key is in Zotero.
[TODO-cite: Frenster et al. 2026, Nat. Cell Biol. 28:875–889, Fig. 2m–n, p. to check; fluctuation-test paper, Cell 2026, p. to check]{.highlight}

Proxies until a count is found:

- **Single-cell counterpart.** The multiome samples give a lower bound:
  384 gastruloids collected at 48 h, frozen at 180,000 cells per vial
  (p. 24). So $N_{48}\ge180{,}000/384\approx470$ cells, at one vial.
  The scRNA-seq time course sorted 12,000 live cells per sample, which
  says nothing about $N_t$ unless the number of pooled gastruloids is
  known. Ask the authors.
- **Exponential interpolation (an assumption, for illustration only).**
  From 300 cells at 0 h to about 15,000–20,000 at 120 h, the doubling
  time is about 20 h. That gives $N_t$ of roughly 1,400–1,600 at 48 h,
  3,100–3,700 at 72 h and 6,900–8,600 at 96 h.
- **No external value.** With the `r glossary("mean scale")`
  $c_i=a_in_i$ and the `r glossary("variance scale")` $\phi_i=a_i^{2}n_i$
  fitted, $\hat n_i=c_i^{2}/\phi_i$ and $\hat a_i=\phi_i/c_i$. An
  external $n_i$ then checks the fitted within-type covariance rather
  than entering the fit.
:::

::: {.highlight}
**TODO: ambient RNA in the single-cell reference (PRJNA954812, GSE229513).**

The deposited data are enough to find ambient RNA, but only after
reprocessing the FASTQs. I read the ENA run reports and searched the
Suppinger PDF; NCBI's GEO and SRA pages blocked automated access, so the
GEO supplementary file lists were not seen.

*What is deposited.* Each single-cell run has two FASTQ files, and the
reads are 84 bp in total: 28 bp of Read 1 plus 56 bp of Read 2, the
read lengths the methods give (p. 24). So Read 1, which holds the cell
barcode and UMI, was kept. Those are the original 10x reads, not just a
filtered matrix.

| Run | Sample | Reads | Bases |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| SRR24173997 | S2_48h | 253 M | 21.3 Gb |
| SRR24564347 | SBR-48h | 163 M | 13.7 Gb |
| SRR24564345 | SBR-72h | 165 M | 13.8 Gb |
| SRR24173994 | S6_96h | 252 M | 21.2 Gb |

Each time point we use has one or two libraries: 48 h has two (S2 and
SBR), 72 h and 96 h one each.

*Why the matrix we use cannot show it.* The object we read from GEO is
the authors' processed Seurat object. It holds only called cells, so
the empty droplets are already gone.

*How to recover it.*

- Re-run STARsolo (or Cell Ranger ≥ 3, or kallisto|bustools) on the
  FASTQs with the 10x v3 barcode whitelist, keeping the unfiltered
  barcode matrix.
- Droplets with very few UMIs give the ambient ("soup") profile, as used
  by `DropletUtils::emptyDrops`.
- SoupX, CellBender or DecontX then estimate the contamination of each
  called cell.

The methods name Cell Ranger 1.3.0 with v3 chemistry, which looks
inconsistent. Reprocessing removes that doubt.

*Ambient RNA as a stand-in for spike-ins.* Ambient RNA could act as a
spike-in for the technical size factor. Every droplet captures the same
soup, so in a cell-containing droplet the ambient counts scale with that
droplet's capture efficiency. Take genes that are abundant in the soup
but not expressed by type $j$, for example markers of other types;
SoupX already uses such genes to estimate contamination. Across the
cells of type $j$:

- their ambient counts, after removing the Poisson variance, give an
  estimate of $\nu^{\mathrm{tech}}$;
- that collapses the $\kappa$ bracket to a single value.

Two caveats:

- **Use counts, not contamination fractions.** The fraction also depends
  on how much RNA the cell itself contributes, so it would bring the
  biological size back in.
- **The soup must be shared.** Each library has its own soup, so
  estimate it per library.

Live-cell FACS sorting with DRAQ7 (12,000 live cells per sample, p. 24)
reduces ambient RNA but does not remove it.
:::

#| label: cov-bulk-depth-call
#| eval: false
# Not run. Bulk depth per cell a_i of the standard-Wnt samples
# (GSE229386) against the scored reference cells of the matched time.
source("R/02_00_utils.R")
source("R/02_01_stats_quality_control.R")
htseq <- read_bulk_htseq(
  "data/raw/GSE229386_AllHTSeqCountsWithGeneNames.txt.gz"
)
# HTSeq summary rows (__no_feature, __ambiguous, ...) are not genes.
is_gene <- !startsWith(rownames(htseq$counts), "__")
slots <- readRDS("output/feature_selection/tier_01/scored_slots.rds")
# TODO: cells per gastruloid x gastruloids per bulk sample, from the
# Suppinger et al. 2023 methods.
cells_per_bulk <- NA_real_
bulk_depth <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(c("48h", "72h", "96h"), function(tm) {
    samples <- standard_wnt_samples(colnames(htseq$counts), tm)
    y_total <- colSums(htseq$counts[is_gene, samples, drop = FALSE])
    s_ref <- stats::median(slots$slots[[tm]]$library_size)
    data.frame(
      time_point = tm,
      sample = samples,
      bulk_counts = y_total,
      ref_median_umi = s_ref,
      a = (y_total / cells_per_bulk) / s_ref
    )
  })
)

## Estimators as run {#sec-cov-estimators}

Every arm keeps the sample variances and regularises the correlation
only. With $\boldsymbol{D}_j$ the sample variances and
$\boldsymbol{R}_j$ the sample correlation of type $j$ at one time,

$$
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j}
=
\boldsymbol{D}_j^{1/2}\,\widetilde{\boldsymbol{R}}_j\,\boldsymbol{D}_j^{1/2},
$$ {#eq-cov-correlation-scale}

with $\widetilde{\boldsymbol{R}}_j$ one of the forms of
@tbl-cov-estimators. No arm penalises the diagonal; the reason is in
[3.2, diagonal](https://bastienchassagnol.github.io/DeCovarT/articles/03-2-covariance-network-estimation.html#sec-cov-diagonal).
`build_sigma()` builds @eq-cov-correlation-scale from the stored
moments. In the shrinkage arms a gene with no variance in a type gets
$10^{-4}$ times the median variance of that type. The factor arm uses
the scale of its own fit, the `r glossary("Poisson floor")` of
@sec-cov-cv-run, so that $\boldsymbol{B}_j\boldsymbol{B}_j^{\top}+\boldsymbol{\Psi}_j$
maps back to the variances the factors were fitted on. The shrinkage
plug-in of the deconvolution is unchanged by that floor.

| Arm | $\widetilde{\boldsymbol{R}}_j$ | Tuning value | Grid | Free covariance parameters, $G$ genes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Diagonal | $\boldsymbol{I}$ | none ($\lambda=1$, or rank 0) | — | $G$ |
| Shrinkage | $(1-\lambda)\boldsymbol{R}_j+\lambda\boldsymbol{I}$ | $\lambda$, per type or one per time | 43 values: 13 log-spaced from $10^{-3}$ to 0.1, then 0.125 to 1 by $1/32$, and 0.9 | no count |
| Two-parameter | $(1-\lambda)\{(1-\alpha)\boldsymbol{R}_j+\alpha\bar{\boldsymbol{R}}\}+\lambda\boldsymbol{I}$ | $(\alpha,\lambda)$, per type or one pair per time | $\alpha\in\{0.25,0.5,0.75\}$ × the 43 levels | no count |
| Factor analysis, per type | $\boldsymbol{B}_j\boldsymbol{B}_j^{\top}+\boldsymbol{\Psi}_j$ | rank $q_j$ | $\{0,1,2,3,5,8,12,20,30\}$ | $G+q_jG-q_j(q_j-1)/2$ |
| Factor analysis, shared loadings | $\boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{B}^{\top}+\boldsymbol{\Psi}_j$ | rank $q$, one per time | $\{0,1,2,3,5,8,12,20\}$ | $JG+qG-q(q-1)/2$ for the $J$ types |

: The arms, on the correlation scale of @eq-cov-correlation-scale. $\bar{\boldsymbol{R}}$: pooled within-type correlation of the time. The grids are set in `scripts/03_04_cv_covariance.R`. {#tbl-cov-estimators}

### Shrinkage covariance {#sec-shrinkage}

$(1-\lambda)\boldsymbol{R}_j+\lambda\boldsymbol{I}$ is the
Schäfer–Strimmer target D: variances kept, every correlation multiplied
by $1-\lambda$ [@schäferShrinkageApproachLargescale2005]
[TODO-cite: Schäfer and Strimmer 2005, target D; p. to check]{.highlight}.
$\lambda$, the `r glossary("shrinkage intensity")`, is
chosen on held-out cells (@sec-cov-cv-run), either per type or as one
level common to the types of a time. The closed-form level is archived
(@sec-cov-archived). The estimate is positive definite for every
$\lambda>0$, whatever $C_j$ and $G_t$; the smallest level of the grid
is $10^{-3}$. The theory is in
[3.2, shrinkage](https://bastienchassagnol.github.io/DeCovarT/articles/03-2-covariance-network-estimation.html#sec-cov-shrinkage).

### Two-parameter shrinkage {#sec-cov-two-param}

$\bar{\boldsymbol{R}}$ is the correlation of
$\boldsymbol{W}=\sum_j (C_j-1)\boldsymbol{V}_j/(N-J)$, with
$\boldsymbol{V}_j$ the sample covariance of type $j$ and $N$ the cells
of the $J$ types of one time and one gene set
(`pooled_correlation()`). $\boldsymbol{W}$ is the tied covariance of
linear discriminant analysis. $\alpha$ moves $\boldsymbol{R}_j$ towards
$\bar{\boldsymbol{R}}$; $\lambda$ then moves the result towards
$\boldsymbol{I}$. This is the family of regularised discriminant
analysis
[TODO-cite: Friedman 1989, Regularized discriminant analysis, Journal of the American Statistical Association; p. to check]{.highlight}
[TODO-cite: Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman 2009, The Elements of Statistical Learning, 2nd ed., Springer; ch. 4, sec. 4.3.1, p. 112, eqs. 4.13–4.14]{.highlight}.
In cross-validation $\bar{\boldsymbol{R}}$ never contains the held-out
cells of the type being scored.

$\bar{\boldsymbol{R}}$ alone is not an arm. It has $G_t(G_t-1)/2$ free
correlations, `r f1(min(pairs_m))` to `r f1(max(pairs_m))` million,
for `r big(min(cells_time))` to `r big(max(cells_time))` cells per time.
At 96 h it is singular: $\boldsymbol{W}$ has rank at most
$N-J$ = `r big(rank_w_96)`, for `r big(n_welch[["96h"]])` genes. It
enters only as a target, with $\alpha<1$ and $\lambda>0$.

### Factor analysis {#sec-cov-factor}

`fit_factor_correlation()` fits
$\boldsymbol{R}_j\approx\boldsymbol{B}_j\boldsymbol{B}_j^{\top}+\boldsymbol{\Psi}_j$
with $q_j$ factors by maximum likelihood, with the EM steps of Rubin and
Thayer [TODO-cite: Rubin and Thayer 1982, EM algorithms for ML factor analysis, Psychometrika; p. to check]{.highlight}.
The columns of $\boldsymbol{B}_j$ are the
`r glossary("factor loading", "factor loadings")` and the diagonal
$\boldsymbol{\Psi}_j$ holds the `r glossary("uniqueness", "uniquenesses")`.
The steps are written on the cells, so the $G\times G$ correlation is
never formed. The cells are standardised with the Poisson floor of
@sec-cov-cv-run. The start is the probabilistic PCA solution; EM stops
after 200 steps. Uniquenesses are floored at 0.01: with fewer cells
than genes the likelihood is unbounded when one of them tends to zero.
Rank 0 is the diagonal model.

`fit_factor_shared()` fits
$\boldsymbol{R}_j\approx\boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{B}^{\top}+\boldsymbol{\Psi}_j$:
the types of one time share the loadings and keep their own
uniquenesses ("same axes, own volumes"). It alternates closed-form
updates of the rows of $\boldsymbol{B}$ and of each
$\boldsymbol{\Psi}_j$, for at most 100 steps.

A factor model on $G$ genes has $G+qG-q(q-1)/2$ free covariance
parameters: loadings up to rotation, plus uniquenesses
[TODO-cite: Murphy 2012, Machine Learning: A Probabilistic Perspective, MIT Press; ch. 12, sec. 12.1.3, p. 384]{.highlight}.
Shared loadings are counted once, plus one uniqueness vector per type.
A rank is used only if it is at most the training cells minus two, at
most the rank of the training correlation, and leaves no more
parameters than the $G(G+1)/2$ entries of the matrix. Rank 30 is
therefore never fitted for the 29-cell somite differentiation front.

### Archived arms {#sec-cov-archived}

These arms are not run in the current pipeline. Their code and a
README are in `scripts/archives/sparse_precision_arms/` and
`scripts/archives/denoised_covariance/`.

**Sparse precisions.** The graphical lasso with an unpenalised
diagonal (`glasso`, EBIC path), the `SILGGM` support with a refit, and
`PLNnetwork`, a Poisson log-normal model with the full-library offset
$\log s_c$ and a latent precision $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_z^{-1}$
penalised off the diagonal:

$$
x_{gc}\mid\boldsymbol{z}_{\cdot c}\sim\mathrm{Poisson}\bigl(s_{c}e^{z_{gc}}\bigr),
\qquad
\boldsymbol{z}_{\cdot c}\sim\mathcal{N}_{G}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{z},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{z}).
$$ {#eq-pln}

None was run on the gated panel. The pipeline now regularises
covariances only; these precision estimators may return as a
sensitivity analysis. Theory:
[3.2, graphical lasso](https://bastienchassagnol.github.io/DeCovarT/articles/03-2-covariance-network-estimation.html#sec-cov-glasso),
[3.2, PLN](https://bastienchassagnol.github.io/DeCovarT/articles/03-2-covariance-network-estimation.html#sec-cov-pln).

- **Denoised covariance.** The Poisson diagonal and a share $\kappa$
  of the size term removed from the sample covariance, $\kappa$
  bracketed between 0 and $\hat\nu/(1+\hat\nu)$, with $\hat\nu$ from
  `extrinsic_noise_nu()`
  ([3.2, raw or denoised](https://bastienchassagnol.github.io/DeCovarT/articles/03-2-covariance-network-estimation.html#sec-raw-vs-denoised)).
  It gave the worst deconvolution of the second pass: RMSE
  `r f2(denoised_96)` at 96 h, Welch panel. These second-pass results
  are kept in `output/deconvolution/second_pass/` and are still read by
  @sec-deconv-fixed-results.
- **Closed-form shrinkage level.** The Schäfer–Strimmer
  $\hat\lambda^{\ast}$ of `corpcor` minimises a
  `r glossary("Frobenius risk")`, not the Gaussian likelihood that
  DeCovarT evaluates. In the first pass it was
  `r span(first_pass$lambda_star[first_pass$cells >= 3000], f3)` for the
  `r sum(first_pass$cells >= 3000)` units with
  `r big(min(first_pass$cells[first_pass$cells >= 3000]))` cells or more,
  and `r span(first_pass$lambda_star[first_pass$cells < 100])` for the
  units with `r min(first_pass$cells)` to
  `r max(first_pass$cells[first_pass$cells < 100])` cells
  (`output/deconvolution/second_pass/plugin_summary_first_pass.csv`).

## Cross-validation and outputs {#sec-cov-cv-run}

One loss selects every tuning value and compares the arms: the
`r glossary("held-out log-score", "held-out Gaussian log-score")` on
the linear scale. For held-out cells
$\mathcal{T}$ and an estimate
$(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}},\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}})$ fitted
without them,

$$
\ell(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}},\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}};\mathcal{T})
=
\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}|}\sum_{c\in\mathcal{T}}
\log\phi_{G}\bigl(\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot c};\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}},\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\bigr).
$$ {#eq-heldout-loglik}

Its expectation is maximised at the true mean and covariance whatever
the law of the cells (Stein's loss), so it is a legitimate loss even
though cells are not Gaussian
([3.2, Gaussian log-score](https://bastienchassagnol.github.io/DeCovarT/articles/03-2-covariance-network-estimation.html#prp-gaussian-logscore)).
Why it replaces AIC, BIC and EBIC as the selector is in
[3.2, cross-validation](https://bastienchassagnol.github.io/DeCovarT/articles/03-2-covariance-network-estimation.html#sec-cov-cv).
The bulk samples are never read.

**Folds.** Leave-one-out under 100 cells (the 36 and 66 naïve cells at
48 h and 72 h, the 29-cell somite front), 5-fold otherwise. The
two-parameter arm uses 5 folds in every unit. Shared loadings use 5
joint folds, each type split into 5. Folds split the cells of one unit:
the score measures generalisation to new cells of this specimen, not
to new specimens (@nte-pseudoreplication).

[TODO (reply to Elias, 2026-11-22): complement the held-out log-score by the
universal approximate cross-validation (UACV) of Commenges et al. (2015),
which approximates leave-one-out without refitting and corrects for a
misspecified or penalised fit, and report its tracking interval
$\Delta_{\mathrm{UACV}}\pm1.96\,\hat\omega/\sqrt{n}$ when two arms or two
models are compared. The interval is asymptotic only, and its unit must be
an independent one: cells of one specimen are pseudo-replicates, and three
bulk replicates per time are too few for a stable variance.]{.highlight}

**Poisson floor.** `split_standardise()`
(`R/03_01_stats_covariance_estimation.R`) standardises the training and
test cells with the training mean $\bar x_g$ and standard deviation
$s_g$ of each gene, with the variance floored at its Poisson level plus
one count over the $C_{\mathrm{tr}}$ training cells:

$$
s_g^{2}=\max\Bigl(v_g,\ \bar x_g+\tfrac{1}{C_{\mathrm{tr}}}\Bigr),
$$ {#eq-cov-poisson-floor}

with $v_g$ the sample variance. A count cannot vary less than a Poisson
count; a smaller variance means too few cells, or the fractional counts
left by ambient-RNA correction. The floor replaced a defect found in the
shared-loadings arm. Before it, the held-out score of the 29-cell somite
differentiation front at 96 h (outer fold 2 of the nested comparison)
was about $-5\times10^{10}$. The gene *Fnbp1* has fractional
ambient-corrected counts in that type: training mean $4\times10^{-7}$,
standard deviation $1.9\times10^{-6}$. One count in a test cell then cost
about $6\times10^{11}$. With the floor that fold scores −9,260, and the
other types move by less than 0.3%. These values come from the
diagnosis of the defect, not from the tables below. The factor fits use
the same scale (`build_sigma()`, @sec-cov-estimators); the shrinkage
plug-in of the deconvolution is unchanged. The tables of
@sec-cov-results-discussion come from the rerun with the floor
(`r cv_date`).

**One spectral decomposition per training set.** The test cells are
standardised with the training means and the floored standard
deviations $s_g$ of @eq-cov-poisson-floor. Let
$\boldsymbol{R}=\sum_{i\le r}\ell_i\boldsymbol{v}_i\boldsymbol{v}_i^{\top}$
be the training correlation, of rank $r$ on $G$ genes. The eigenvectors
of $(1-\lambda)\boldsymbol{R}+\lambda\boldsymbol{I}$ do not depend on
$\lambda$; its eigenvalues are $e_i=(1-\lambda)\ell_i+\lambda$ on the
range and $\lambda$ on the null space. For a standardised test cell
$\boldsymbol{z}$,

$$
\log\phi
=
-\tfrac12\Bigl[
G\log 2\pi+2\sum_g\log s_g
+\sum_{i\le r}\log e_i+(G-r)\log\lambda
+\sum_{i\le r}\frac{(\boldsymbol{v}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{z})^{2}}{e_i}
+\frac{\lVert\boldsymbol{z}\rVert^{2}-\sum_{i\le r}(\boldsymbol{v}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{z})^{2}}{\lambda}
\Bigr].
$$ {#eq-cov-path-score}

<!-- chk: R1, R2 -->

One decomposition therefore scores the `r n_levels` levels
(`spectral_path_core()`). It is taken on the smaller of
$\boldsymbol{Z}\boldsymbol{Z}^{\top}$ and
$\boldsymbol{Z}^{\top}\boldsymbol{Z}$, with $\boldsymbol{Z}$ the
standardised training cells. The two-parameter arm needs one
decomposition per $\alpha$.

**Factor scores.** With
$\boldsymbol{M}=\boldsymbol{I}+\boldsymbol{B}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Psi}^{-1}\boldsymbol{B}$,
of size $q\times q$,

$$
(\boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{B}^{\top}+\boldsymbol{\Psi})^{-1}
=
\boldsymbol{\Psi}^{-1}-\boldsymbol{\Psi}^{-1}\boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{M}^{-1}\boldsymbol{B}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Psi}^{-1},
\qquad
\det(\boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{B}^{\top}+\boldsymbol{\Psi})
=
\det\boldsymbol{\Psi}\,\det\boldsymbol{M}
$$ {#eq-cov-woodbury}

<!-- chk: R3 -->

(`factor_core()`). No $G\times G$ matrix is factorised.

**Constant genes.** A gene constant in a training set is scored apart,
as an independent Gaussian with the variance of
@eq-cov-poisson-floor. That part of the score is the same for every
tuning value; it is left out of the fold-to-fold spread.

**Rules.**

- *Per type:* the value with the highest mean held-out score (`min`).
  The one-standard-error choice, the most regularised value within one
  standard error of that maximum, is reported beside it (`1se`).
- *Common:* one value per time, the one with the highest sum over types
  of the mean held-out score. For shared loadings this is the only rule.

**Nested comparison.** A `r glossary("nested cross-validation")`: the
cells of each time are split into 5 outer folds, stratified by type. Each rule chooses its tuning value on the
outer training cells only, with the folds above, and is scored on the
outer test cells. Scores are paired by fold and type; the gain is
reported against the diagonal model.

**Information criteria.** The factor models are refitted on all cells
of each unit (stage `fit`; these fits enter the deconvolution). AIC
and BIC are computed from the free-parameter counts of
@tbl-cov-estimators, plus $G$ means per type. They are reported, not
used to select.

**Grid search only.** Every tuning value is chosen on a fixed grid.
With one or two tuning parameters a grid is as reliable as random
search, whose advantage appears when few of many hyperparameters matter
[TODO-cite: Bergstra and Bengio 2012, Random search for
hyper-parameter optimization, Journal of Machine Learning Research
13:281–305; p. 283]{.highlight}. Here the shrinkage "path" is itself a
grid, of `r n_levels` levels, scored from one spectral decomposition
per fold (@eq-cov-path-score); the two-parameter arm adds one
decomposition per $\alpha$. The former `search` stage compared, on 5
folds, the exact path on 200 levels, a 10-value grid with one Cholesky
factor per value, `optimize()` on the path over $[10^{-3},1]$ and 10
random levels; for the two-parameter arm, on panels of at most 1,500
genes, a $5\times8$ grid in $(\alpha,\lambda)$ against 40 random pairs.
It is archived in `scripts/archives/search_comparison/` (see its
README); its table, `output/grn/cv/search_comparison.csv`, is still read
here (@sec-cov-search-results). The loss of a strategy is the held-out
score of the best path value minus that of its choice.

```pseudocode
#| label: algo-cv-covariance
#| html-line-number: true
#| pdf-line-number: true

\begin{algorithm}
\caption{Held-out scores along the paths, selection, and nested comparison}
\begin{algorithmic}
\Procedure{PathScores}{$X_{\mathrm{train}}, X_{\mathrm{test}}, \Lambda, Q, A$}
  \State standardise both sets with the training means and standard deviations
  \State $(\ell, V) \gets$ non-zero spectrum of the training correlation $R$
  \For{$\lambda \in \Lambda$}
    \State $s(\lambda) \gets$ mean path score of the test cells, from $(\ell, V)$
  \EndFor
  \For{$q \in Q$}
    \State $(B, \Psi) \gets$ \Call{FactorEM}{$X_{\mathrm{train}}, q$}, started from $(\ell, V)$
    \State $s(q) \gets$ mean test score through the Woodbury identity
  \EndFor
  \For{$\alpha \in A$}
    \State spectrum of $(1-\alpha)R + \alpha\bar R$; $s(\alpha,\lambda)$ for every $\lambda \in \Lambda$
  \EndFor
  \State \Return $s$
\EndProcedure
\Procedure{Select}{$X$, folds}
  \For{each fold $k$}
    \State $s_k \gets$ \Call{PathScores}{$X_{-k}, X_k, \Lambda, Q, A$}
  \EndFor
  \State $m \gets$ mean of $s_k$ over folds
  \State \Return $\arg\max m$ per type; $\arg\max \sum_j m_j$ for a common value
\EndProcedure
\Procedure{NestedCompare}{$X_1,\ldots,X_J$}
  \State split each $X_j$ into 5 outer folds
  \For{$k = 1,\ldots,5$}
    \For{each rule $e$}
      \State choose its value by \Call{Select}{} on the outer training cells
      \State $g_{ek} \gets$ test score of rule $e$ $-$ test score of the diagonal
    \EndFor
  \EndFor
  \State \Return $(g_{ek})$, paired by fold
\EndProcedure
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}
```

Outputs in `output/grn/cv/`:

- `cv_tuning_scores.csv`: mean and standard error of the held-out
  score for each unit, arm and tuning value;
- `cv_selected_tuning.csv`: the value chosen by each rule
  (@tbl-cov-lambda);
- `nested_cv_by_fold.csv`, `nested_cv_summary.csv`: outer-fold scores
  and gains over the diagonal (@tbl-cov-nested);
- `information_criteria.csv`: log-likelihood, parameters, AIC, BIC and
  EM convergence per factor rank;
- `search_comparison.csv`: choice, loss and time of each search
  strategy (@tbl-cov-search), written by the archived `search` stage and
  not rewritten by the current script.

Every file covers the three panels. @tbl-cov-lambda and
@tbl-cov-nested show the Welch panel; @tbl-cov-panels gives the
choices made once per time on all three.

> For the arm and tuning value retained,
$\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j}$ is the mean of the raw counts of
the cells of type $j$, and $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j}$ is
@eq-cov-correlation-scale, both on the scale of @sec-cov-inputs. It is
positive definite because $\lambda>0$ or $\boldsymbol{\Psi}_j\succ0$,
so @eq-grn-export holds by construction. Which covariance layer these
cell-level moments identify, and how the sample scales are estimated
inside the DeCovarT fit, is in
[2.1, three regimes](https://bastienchassagnol.github.io/DeCovarT/articles/02-1-single-cell-generative-optimisation.html#sec-three-regimes)
and
[2.1, profile Newton](https://bastienchassagnol.github.io/DeCovarT/articles/02-1-single-cell-generative-optimisation.html#sec-profile-newton).

## Results and discussion {#sec-cov-results-discussion}

### Regularisation shrinks covariance terms without setting them to zero {#sec-cov-shrinkage-reading}

**What the shrinkage arm returns.** The estimate is
$\boldsymbol{D}_j^{1/2}\{(1-\lambda)\boldsymbol{R}_j+\lambda\boldsymbol{I}\}\boldsymbol{D}_j^{1/2}$
(@sec-shrinkage). Three readings follow.

- **Variances are untouched.** Only the correlations move.
- **Every correlation is multiplied by $1-\lambda$; none becomes
  zero.** The estimate has as many non-zero off-diagonal terms as the
  sample covariance: all $G_t(G_t-1)/2$ pairs, that is
  `r and_list(paste(f1(pairs_m), "million at", hours(names(pairs_m))))`
  on the Welch panel. Its inverse is dense as well, so no graph can be read from
  either matrix. The factor models are dense too: each off-diagonal
  term is an entry of $\boldsymbol{B}_j\boldsymbol{B}_j^{\top}$.
- **$\lambda$ is a floor on the spectrum.** Each eigenvalue $\ell$ of
  $\boldsymbol{R}_j$ becomes $(1-\lambda)\ell+\lambda$, so the smallest
  eigenvalue of the shrunk correlation is at least $\lambda$. That
  floor makes the estimate positive definite when $C_j\le G_t$.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-cov-lambda
#| tbl-cap: "Tuning values chosen on held-out cells, Welch panel (`output/grn/cv/cv_selected_tuning.csv`). $C_j$: scored cells. Shrinkage: level $\\lambda$ per type (`min` and `1se`) and common to the types of a time. Two-parameter: $(\\alpha,\\lambda)$ per type and common. Factor rank: per type, and shared by the types of a time. Leave-one-out for $C_j<100$, 5-fold otherwise."
#| echo: false
cv_dir <- here::here("..", "output", "grn", "cv")
sel <- utils::read.csv(
  file.path(cv_dir, "cv_selected_tuning.csv"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  fileEncoding = "UTF-8"
)
sel <- sel[sel$gene_set == "welch", , drop = FALSE]
units <- utils::read.csv(
  here::here("..", "output", "grn", "plugin", "plugin_summary.csv"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  fileEncoding = "UTF-8"
)
units <- unique(units[units$gene_set == "welch", , drop = FALSE])
units <- units[order(units$time_point, -units$cells), , drop = FALSE]
unit_key <- paste(units$time_point, units$cell_type)
pick <- function(rule, column = "tuning") {
  d <- sel[sel$rule == rule, , drop = FALSE]
  d[[column]][match(unit_key, paste(d$time, d$cell_type))]
}
f2 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)
pair <- function(rule) {
  paste0("(", f2(pick(rule, "alpha")), ", ", f2(pick(rule)), ")")
}
tab <- data.frame(
  sub("h$", " h", units$time_point),
  units$cell_type,
  format(units$cells, big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE),
  f2(pick("shrinkage, per type")),
  f2(pick("shrinkage, per type, 1se")),
  f2(pick("shrinkage, common")),
  pair("two-parameter, per type"),
  pair("two-parameter, common"),
  as.character(pick("factor, per type")),
  as.character(pick("factor, shared loadings"))
)
colnames(tab) <- c(
  "Time",
  "Cell type",
  "$C_j$",
  "Per type",
  "Per type, 1se",
  "Common",
  "Per type",
  "Common",
  "Per type",
  "Shared"
)
tinytable::tt(tab) |>
  tinytable::group_tt(
    j = list(
      "Shrinkage $\\lambda$" = 4:6,
      "Two-parameter $(\\alpha,\\lambda)$" = 7:8,
      "Factor rank" = 9:10
    )
  ) |>
  tinytable::format_tt(quarto = TRUE) |>
  tinytable::style_tt(j = 3:10, align = "r")
```

- **Held-out cells choose strong shrinkage.** The per-type level is
  `r f2(epi48)` for the 48 h epiblast, `r span(lam_big)` for the other
  types with 1,000 cells or more, and `r span(lam_small)` for the types
  with fewer. Except in the 48 h epiblast, each sample correlation keeps
  `r span(1 - shr_rest$tuning, pct)` of its value. The common level is
  `r and_list(paste(f2(common_w$tuning), "at", hours(common_w$time)))`.
  The `1se` rule picks $\lambda=1$, the diagonal, for
  `r if (nrow(one_se_diag)) and_list(unit_the(one_se_diag$time, one_se_diag$cell_type)) else "no unit"`.
- **The two-parameter arm pools as much as the grid allows.**
  $\alpha=0.75$, the largest value of the grid, in
  `r sum(tp_all$alpha == 0.75)` of the `r nrow(tp_all)` Welch choices,
  per type and common. Its $\lambda$ is no higher than that of plain
  shrinkage: `r span(tp_type$tuning)` per type.
- **Factor ranks follow the number of cells.** Rank
  `r max(fa_w$tuning)`, the edge of the grid, for
  `r and_list(unit_the(fa_top$time, fa_top$cell_type))`; ranks
  `r min(fa_small$tuning)` to `r max(fa_small$tuning)` for the types
  with fewer than 1,000 cells. Shared loadings choose rank
  `r and_list(paste(shared_w$tuning, "at", hours(shared_w$time)))`.
- **The shared rank and the Poisson floor.** Before the floor of
  @eq-cov-poisson-floor, the shared-loadings scores of the two rarest
  types were of order $-10^{7}$ (36 naïve cells, 48 h) and $-10^{10}$
  (somite front, 96 h) at every rank, rank 0 included, against
  $-2.4\times10^{3}$ and $-2.2\times10^{4}$ for the same diagonal model
  scored by leave-one-out. The somite front then decided the sum over
  types and set the 96 h shared rank. The cause at 96 h was one gene
  with fractional counts (@sec-cov-cv-run); the 48 h case was not traced
  separately. With the floor (tables of `r cv_date`) shared loadings
  choose rank `r shared_top`, the largest of their grid, at
  `r and_list(unique(hours(shared_all$time[shared_all$gene_set %in% c("welch", "r2_01") & shared_all$tuning == shared_top])))`
  on the Welch and $R^2_D\ge 1\%$ panels (@tbl-cov-panels). The rank
  is not interior there; the grid must be extended before the shared
  loadings are compared with the other arms.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-cov-panels
#| tbl-cap: "Choices made once per time, on the three panels (`output/grn/cv/cv_selected_tuning.csv`). $G_t$: panel genes. Common: the level, or pair, with the highest held-out score summed over the types of the time; shared: rank of the shared loadings; per type: range of the per-type factor ranks. Last column: shrinkage level chosen by the bulk likelihood summed over the three standard-Wnt replicates (`output/deconvolution/lambda_selection.csv`, @sec-deconv-selection)."
#| echo: false
panel_name <- c(welch = "Welch", r2_01 = "$R^2_D\\ge 1\\%$", r2_05 = "$R^2_D\\ge 5\\%$")
slot_tab <- unique(sel_all[c("gene_set", "time")])
slot_tab <- slot_tab[order(match(slot_tab$gene_set, names(panel_name)), slot_tab$time), ]
one <- function(rule, gs, tm, k = "tuning") {
  sel_all[[k]][sel_all$rule == rule & sel_all$gene_set == gs & sel_all$time == tm][[1L]]
}
tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(slot_tab)), function(i) {
  gs <- slot_tab$gene_set[[i]]
  tm <- slot_tab$time[[i]]
  fr <- sel_all$tuning[sel_all$rule == "factor, per type" & sel_all$gene_set == gs & sel_all$time == tm]
  data.frame(
    panel_name[[gs]], hours(tm),
    big(sum(gene_sets$gene_set == gs & gene_sets$time_point == tm)),
    f2(one("shrinkage, common", gs, tm)),
    paste0("(", f2(one("two-parameter, common", gs, tm, "alpha")), ", ",
           f2(one("two-parameter, common", gs, tm)), ")"),
    format(one("factor, shared loadings", gs, tm)),
    paste(min(fr), "to", max(fr)),
    format(bulk_lam$tuning[bulk_lam$gene_set == gs & bulk_lam$time == tm])
  )
}))
colnames(tab) <- c(
  "Panel", "Time", "$G_t$", "Common $\\lambda$", "Common $(\\alpha,\\lambda)$",
  "Shared", "Per type", "Bulk likelihood $\\lambda$"
)
tinytable::tt(tab) |>
  tinytable::group_tt(j = list("Shrinkage" = 4:5, "Factor rank" = 6:7)) |>
  tinytable::format_tt(quarto = TRUE) |>
  tinytable::style_tt(j = 3:8, align = "r")
```

- **The common level is far above what the bulk chooses.** Held-out
  cells choose a common shrinkage level of
  `r span(common_all$tuning)` across panels and times
  (@tbl-cov-panels). The bulk likelihood chooses `r span(bulk_wr)` on
  the Welch and $R^2_D\ge 1\%$ panels, and
  `r and_list(paste(format(bulk_05$tuning), "at", hours(bulk_05$time)))`
  on the $R^2_D\ge 5\%$ panel, whose 48 h slot has
  `r n_r2_05[["48h"]]` genes.
- **Shared loadings sit at the top of their grid**, rank
  `r shared_top`, in `r sum(shared_all$tuning == shared_top)` of the
  `r nrow(shared_all)` slots; the per-type rank is
  `r max(sel_all$tuning[sel_all$rule == "factor, per type"])`, the top
  of its grid, in
  `r sum(sel_all$rule == "factor, per type" & sel_all$tuning == max(scores$tuning[scores$arm == "factor"]))`
  of the `r sum(sel_all$rule == "factor, per type")` type × time × panel
  units.

**A dense estimate is not evidence that every pair of genes
interacts.** Three mechanisms give a non-zero covariance to a pair
with no direct link.

- **Sampling noise.** A sample correlation is never exactly zero, even
  for independent genes. Shrinkage multiplies it by $1-\lambda$; it
  does not threshold.
- **Covariance is not the network.** Direct interactions are the zeros
  of the precision matrix. Two genes linked only through other genes
  still have a non-zero covariance. A covariance block is zero only
  between groups of genes with no path between them. Isolated groups
  could be looked for with the archived sparse arms
  (@sec-cov-archived), not with these.
- **Raw counts share a cell-size factor.** The covariances are computed
  on raw counts (@sec-cov-inputs), so every pair of genes receives the
  size term $\nu\,\mu_g\mu_h$, positive for all pairs. This is the
  extrinsic noise that the archived `extrinsic_noise_nu()` estimated.

### Nested comparison {#sec-cov-nested-results}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-cov-nested
#| tbl-cap: "Gain of each rule over the diagonal model in held-out log-score per cell, Welch panel: mean over the 5 outer folds (standard error), paired by fold (`output/grn/cv/nested_cv_summary.csv`). The tuning value of each rule is chosen on the outer training cells only. Bold: highest mean gain of the unit."
#| echo: false
nested <- utils::read.csv(
  here::here("..", "output", "grn", "cv", "nested_cv_summary.csv"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  fileEncoding = "UTF-8"
)
nested <- nested[nested$gene_set == "welch", , drop = FALSE]
units <- utils::read.csv(
  here::here("..", "output", "grn", "plugin", "plugin_summary.csv"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  fileEncoding = "UTF-8"
)
units <- unique(units[units$gene_set == "welch", , drop = FALSE])
units <- units[order(units$time_point, -units$cells), , drop = FALSE]
rules <- c(
  "shrinkage, per type",
  "shrinkage, common",
  "two-parameter, per type",
  "two-parameter, common",
  "factor, per type",
  "factor, shared loadings"
)
gain <- sapply(rules, function(r) {
  d <- nested[nested$rule == r, , drop = FALSE]
  i <- match(
    paste(units$time_point, units$cell_type),
    paste(d$time, d$cell_type)
  )
  d$mean_gain_over_diagonal[i]
})
se <- sapply(rules, function(r) {
  d <- nested[nested$rule == r, , drop = FALSE]
  i <- match(
    paste(units$time_point, units$cell_type),
    paste(d$time, d$cell_type)
  )
  d$se_gain[i]
})
cells_txt <- matrix(
  paste0(round(gain), " (", round(se), ")"),
  nrow = nrow(gain)
)
tab <- data.frame(
  sub("h$", " h", units$time_point),
  units$cell_type,
  format(units$cells, big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE),
  cells_txt
)
colnames(tab) <- c(
  "Time",
  "Cell type",
  "$C_j$",
  "Per type",
  "Common",
  "Per type",
  "Common",
  "Per type",
  "Shared loadings"
)
out <- tinytable::tt(tab) |>
  tinytable::group_tt(
    j = list("Shrinkage" = 4:5, "Two-parameter" = 6:7, "Factor analysis" = 8:9)
  ) |>
  tinytable::format_tt(quarto = TRUE) |>
  tinytable::style_tt(j = 3:9, align = "r")
best <- apply(gain, 1L, which.max)
for (i in seq_along(best)) {
  out <- tinytable::style_tt(out, i = i, j = 3L + best[[i]], bold = TRUE)
}
out
```

- **Every rule beats the diagonal on average.** The mean gain is
  positive in `r n_positive` of the `r nrow(nested_w)` unit × rule
  cells, and exceeds two standard errors in `r n_two_se`. The
  exceptions are `r if (nrow(weak)) weak_txt else "none"`.
- **Abundant types.** In the units with 1,000 cells or more the rule
  with the highest mean gain is: `r best_txt(best_w[best_w$cells >= 1000, ])`.
- **Rare types.** In the units with fewer than 1,000 cells:
  `r best_txt(best_w[best_w$cells < 1000, ])`. In
  `r sum(borrow[best_w$cells < 1000])` of these
  `r sum(best_w$cells < 1000)` units the best rule borrows across types
  (shared loadings or the two-parameter arm).
- **Common rules and the diagonal.** The common shrinkage and
  two-parameter rules choose $\lambda=1$, the diagonal, in
  `r nrow(diag_folds)` of their `r n_common_choices` time × rule ×
  outer-fold choices (`nested_cv_by_fold.csv`); such a fold widens
  their standard errors.

### Search strategies {#sec-cov-search-results}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-cov-search
#| tbl-cap: "Search strategies for the tuning value, both gene sets pooled (`output/grn/cv/search_comparison.csv`; shrinkage: 22 type × time × gene-set units; two-parameter: the 14 units with at most 1,500 genes). Loss: held-out log-score per cell of the best value found by the reference (the exact path for shrinkage; the better of the two strategies for the two-parameter arm) minus that of the strategy's choice. Time: wall-clock seconds per unit, path preparation included."
#| echo: false
search <- utils::read.csv(
  here::here("..", "output", "grn", "cv", "search_comparison.csv"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  fileEncoding = "UTF-8"
)
plan <- data.frame(
  arm = c(rep("shrinkage", 4L), rep("two_param", 2L)),
  strategy = c(
    "exact path",
    "optimiser on the path",
    "random values on the path",
    "grid, one factorisation per value",
    "grid, path in lambda",
    "random pairs"
  ),
  label = c(
    "Exact path, 200 levels",
    "`optimize()` on the path",
    "10 random levels on the path",
    "10-value grid, one Cholesky factor per value",
    "5 × 8 grid, path in $\\lambda$",
    "40 random pairs"
  ),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
loss_fmt <- function(x) {
  ifelse(
    abs(x) >= 1000,
    format(round(x), big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE),
    formatC(x, format = "fg", digits = 2)
  )
}
rows <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(plan)), function(i) {
  d <- search[
    search$arm == plan$arm[[i]] & search$strategy == plan$strategy[[i]],
    ,
    drop = FALSE
  ]
  data.frame(
    ifelse(plan$arm[[i]] == "shrinkage", "Shrinkage", "Two-parameter"),
    plan$label[[i]],
    nrow(d),
    formatC(stats::median(d$elapsed_sec), format = "f", digits = 2),
    loss_fmt(stats::median(d$score_loss)),
    loss_fmt(max(d$score_loss)),
    sum(d$score_loss > 0.1)
  )
})
tab <- do.call(rbind, rows)
colnames(tab) <- c(
  "Arm",
  "Strategy",
  "Units",
  "Median time (s)",
  "Median loss",
  "Largest loss",
  "Units with loss > 0.1"
)
tinytable::tt(tab) |>
  tinytable::format_tt(quarto = TRUE) |>
  tinytable::style_tt(j = 3:7, align = "r")
```

- **The exact path is the cheapest and the reference.** Median
  `r f2(s_med("shrinkage", "exact path", "elapsed_sec"))` s per unit,
  against `r f1(s_med("shrinkage", "grid, one factorisation per value", "elapsed_sec"))` s
  for a 10-value grid refitted value by value. The refitted grid loses
  `r f2(s_med("shrinkage", "grid, one factorisation per value", "score_loss"))`
  log-score units per cell (median); it loses more than 0.1 in
  `r sum(grid_d$score_loss > 0.1)` of `r nrow(grid_d)` units. Its
  largest loss, `r format(signif(grid_worst$score_loss, 2), big.mark = ",")`,
  is for `r unit_the(grid_worst$time, grid_worst$cell_type)`
  (`r grid_worst$gene_set` panel), whose best level is 1 while that grid
  stops at 0.9. The loss comes from the coarse grid, not from grid
  search: the path is a finer grid.
- **Random levels lose
  `r f2(s_med("shrinkage", "random values on the path", "score_loss"))`
  (median)** for the same cost as the path.
- **`optimize()` on the path matches the path** in
  `r sum(opt_d$score_loss <= 0.01)` of `r nrow(opt_d)` units (loss at
  most 0.01; a negative loss is a level between two path values).
- **Two-parameter arm.** 40 random pairs take
  `r f1(s_med("two_param", "random pairs", "elapsed_sec"))` s per unit
  against `r f1(s_med("two_param", "grid, path in lambda", "elapsed_sec"))` s
  for the $5\times8$ grid, and lose
  `r f2(s_med("two_param", "random pairs", "score_loss"))` (median).
- On the Welch panel alone the times are larger (median
  `r f2(s_med("shrinkage", "exact path", "elapsed_sec", search_w))` s
  for the path,
  `r round(s_med("shrinkage", "grid, one factorisation per value", "elapsed_sec", search_w))` s
  for the refitted grid) and so are the losses (median
  `r f1(s_med("shrinkage", "grid, one factorisation per value", "score_loss", search_w))`
  for the refitted grid).

### Information criteria {#sec-cov-ic-results}

On the Welch panel (`information_criteria.csv`), AIC chooses the
largest fitted rank for `r sum(ic_type$aic == ic_type$top)` of
`r nrow(ic_type)` types, and rank
`r and_list(paste(ic_shared$aic, "at", hours(ic_shared$time)))` for the
shared loadings. BIC chooses ranks `r min(ic_type$bic)` to 8 for
`r sum(ic_type$bic <= 8)` types`r if (nrow(bic_high)) paste0(", and ", and_list(paste(bic_high$bic, "for", unit_the(bic_high$time, bic_high$cell_type))))`.
For the shared loadings BIC chooses
`r and_list(paste(ic_shared$bic, "at", hours(ic_shared$time)))`. Of the
`r sum(ic$arm == "factor")` per-type fits on all cells,
`r sum(ic$arm == "factor" & !ic$converged)` stopped at the 200-step
limit; `r sum(ic$arm != "factor" & ic$converged)` of the
`r sum(ic$arm != "factor")` shared fits converged.

### What this implies for the deconvolution {#sec-cov-deconv-implication}

The acceptance of a dense plug-in (@sec-cov-scope) concerns the
likelihood, not the interpretation. The levels that predict held-out
cells best are too strong for the bulk (@sec-deconv-selection). On the
Welch panel at 96 h the `r glossary("RMSE")` of the proportions is
`r f3(rmse_id("cv_shrinkage_per_type"))` with the per-type levels and
`r f3(rmse_id("cv_shrinkage_common"))` with the common level, against
`r f3(bulk_pick$rmse)` at $\lambda=`r bulk_pick$tuning`$, the level
chosen by the bulk likelihood (`output/deconvolution/lambda_selection.csv`).
